Let S={p-1:p is prime}. In a finite impartial subtraction game, call 0 a P-position, and recursively call m>0 a P-position if every legal move from m goes to an N-position; call it N if some legal move goes to a P-position.

Construct a_1=0 and, after a_1<...<a_{k-1} have been chosen, let a_k be the least integer greater than a_{k-1} such that a_k-a_j is not in S for every j<k. This construction never stops. Indeed, S has arbitrarily long gaps: for every L, the integers (L+1)!+1,...,(L+1)!+L are composite, so the corresponding preceding differences are absent from S. If [x,x+L-1] is a gap in S and D=a_{k-1}, then every translate S+a_j omits [x+a_j,x+a_j+L-1]. Choosing L>D+1, these intervals have the common subinterval [x+D,x+L-1], which contains an integer larger than D missing from every S+a_j. Thus a_k exists, and the sequence is infinite.

We prove by induction on m that m is a P-position exactly when m=a_k for some k. The assertion holds at 0. Suppose it holds for all smaller integers. If m=a_k, then by construction no legal move from m reaches an earlier a_j. Every destination m-s is smaller than m and hence, by induction, is N. Thus m is P. If m is not one of the a_k, let a_k be the first selected value greater than m, or take the stage at which m was considered. Since m was not selected, m-a_j belongs to S for some earlier a_j; hence m has a legal move to a_j, which is P by induction. Therefore m is N.

Consequently all a_k are P-positions, and there are infinitely many of them. If the initial heap has size a_k, Alice starts at a P-position, so Bob has a winning strategy. Hence infinitely many n have the required property. QED.

For each i≤r, the translate S+a_i omits [x+a_i,x+a_i+M-1]. Because 0≤a_i≤D, the intersection of these omitted intervals contains [x+D,x+M-1], which is nonempty. If m=a_i, then no legal destination m-s equals an earlier a_j, by the defining condition. Every destination is smaller than m, so by induction it is N. Thus m is P.
